What if the money advice you learned as a kid is actually keeping you from building wealth?

Saving money, working hard, getting a stable job, and earning a higher salary all sound like smart financial advice. But what if following these childhood money lessons isn't enough to achieve financial freedom?

Most of us grew up learning how to earn money, save money, and avoid unnecessary spending. But we weren't always taught how to increase our earning potential, manage our income, invest wisely, and turn that income into long-term wealth.

In this video, Logical Money breaks down 7 childhood money lessons that can quietly keep you financially stuck — and explains the missing financial principles that can help you get ahead.

Here's what you'll learn:
1. Why saving money alone won't make you wealthy.
2. Why hard work doesn't always lead to higher income.
3. Why wanting more money isn't necessarily greedy.
4. Why being good at your job isn't always enough.
5. Why earning more doesn't automatically make you richer.
6. Why a stable job shouldn't be your entire financial plan.

The financial advice you learned growing up wasn't necessarily wrong.

title: If YOU Are Saving Money, You NEED To Stop!
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
If you’re saving money, you NEED to stop… and ask yourself one question: what exactly are you saving it for?

Saving money is one of the first financial lessons most of us learn.
Earn $100.
Spend $80.
Save $20.
Keep doing that for decades and eventually… you should be rich.
Right? - Not necessarily.

Because saving money and building wealth are not the same thing.
Cash is incredibly useful. It pays your bills, protects you during emergencies, and gives you financial flexibility. But if money is being saved for decades simply to sit as cash, there’s a problem: Inflation gradually reduces its purchasing power.

In this video, Logical Money breaks down:
1. How money actually works.
2. Why money and wealth are different.
3. How banks create money through lending.
4. How inflation affects your savings.
5. How to think about saving vs investing, emergency funds, cash, assets, and long-term wealth building.

We’ll go from the giant stone money of Yap and ancient systems of debt and credit to modern bank deposits and the Federal Reserve's 2% longer-run inflation goal.
And it all leads to one important distinction:
Money is the tool. Wealth is the valuable things that money ultimately allows you to own.

Think about your money as having three different jobs:
NOW — Money for rent, groceries, utility bills, school fees, everyday spending, and other expenses you need to cover now.
SAFETY — Your emergency fund and money you expect to need relatively soon.
WEALTH — Money you don't expect to need for years. This is where the objective can change from simply storing dollars to potentially using those dollars to acquire assets.

Before saving another dollar, understand its job.
Is it for next month's rent?
An emergency fund?
A purchase next year?
Or wealth you want to build over the next 20 or 30 years?
Those are very different financial objectives—and the same strategy doesn't necessarily make sense for all of them.

title: How to Manage Your Money LIKE THE 1%
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
How do the wealthy actually manage their money?

It’s easy to look at the top 1% and focus on what they buy — expensive cars, luxury homes, watches and private jets. But those things didn’t make them wealthy — Ownership did.

In this video, we break down a simple 25–15–50–10 money management framework built around one powerful idea:
Use part of what you earn today to build what you’ll own tomorrow.

Instead of spending your paycheck first and trying to invest whatever happens to be left, this approach gives every part of your income a specific job:
25% GROWTH — Building ownership through long-term investing.
15% STABILITY — Building an emergency fund and protecting your finances.
50% ESSENTIALS — Housing, food, insurance, transportation and everyday living.
10% REWARDS — Actually enjoying some of the money you worked for.

These percentages are not official financial rules, and they won’t fit everyone. Your ideal numbers depend on your income, expenses, debt, family situation and financial goals.
The bigger lesson is the order of priority.

You'll learn:
1. Why automatically investing part of your paycheck can be more effective than waiting to see what’s left.
2. Why diversified low-cost index funds can be useful for long-term investors.
3. How an emergency fund can help prevent you from selling investments at the worst possible time.
4. Why controlling major expenses like housing and transportation can matter far more than obsessing over every $3 coffee.

Whether you're trying to start investing, build an emergency fund, contribute more to your 401(k) or Roth IRA, control lifestyle inflation, reach financial independence, or simply get better at managing your paycheck, the goal is the same — Turn more of your income into things you continue to own.

Because looking rich requires money.
Actually building wealth requires ownership.

title: Why Looking Poor Is SO Important | Logical Money

description:
Why do some people look rich but struggle financially, while others look completely ordinary and quietly build serious wealth?

The answer has less to do with how much money you make and much more to do with what happens to that money after you make it.

In this video, we break down why looking poor can actually be one of the smartest financial decisions you make — and why trying to look wealthy can quietly destroy your ability to actually become wealthy.

Meet Mike and Alex.
Mike has the luxury SUV, expensive watch, latest phone and lifestyle that screams success.
Alex drives an older paid-off Toyota, keeps his phone longer and doesn't seem particularly wealthy from the outside.
But underneath the surface, their finances tell a completely different story.

This video explores lifestyle inflation, the Diderot Effect, compound growth, financial freedom, consumer psychology and the hidden opportunity cost of trying to look successful.

You'll discover why:
1. Looking rich can become surprisingly expensive.
2. Lifestyle creep can absorb even a high income.
3. Lower monthly expenses can give you more financial freedom.
4. Investing relatively small amounts consistently can create significant long-term wealth.
5. Displaying wealth can create financial and social expectations.
6. Learning what “enough” means may be one of the most powerful financial decisions you make.

We also look at a simple example: what happens when one person spends an extra $500 per month on lifestyle upgrades while another invests that money.
At an illustrative 7% annual return, investing $500 every month for 30 years could grow to roughly $610,000 — despite total contributions of only $180,000.

The lesson isn't that you should never buy a nice car, upgrade your house or spend money on things you enjoy.
It's that there is an enormous difference between spending money because something genuinely improves your life and spending money because you want other people to notice your life.

The goal isn't to look poor. The goal is to stop needing to look rich.

title: Buy, Finance or Lease a Car in 2026 — Which Is Cheaper?

description:
A $299 lease payment sounds a lot better than a $624 finance payment. But the monthly payment doesn’t tell you what the car is actually costing you.

In this video, we put cash vs financing vs leasing through the same three-year test using a 2026 Toyota RAV4 and real-world 2026 pricing, financing, lease and depreciation data.

We follow three versions of the same buyer:
Cash Ryan — pays for the car outright
Finance Ryan — puts money down and finances the rest
Lease Ryan — takes the lower monthly payment and returns the vehicle after three years

Then we calculate what really matters:
How much cash actually leaves your pocket?
How much interest do you pay?
How much equity do you build?
What is the car estimated to be worth after three years?
What happens to your liquidity when you pay cash?
What are you really paying for when you lease?

Using the assumptions in our example, the estimated three-year costs come out to roughly:
CASH — $6,500
FINANCE — $10,700
LEASE — $14,500

But that does not automatically mean everyone should pay cash.
Financing preserves liquidity. Leasing can provide convenience, predictable turnover and less exposure to resale-value risk.

And that leads to one of the most important ideas in the video:
The cheapest monthly payment is not necessarily the cheapest way to own or use a car.

We also look at the opportunity cost of paying cash, why APR matters enormously, and why depreciation can completely change the result from one vehicle to another.

And there’s an even bigger question.
Before spending hours optimizing whether you should buy vs lease vs finance, make sure you haven’t overlooked the financial decision that could matter far more:
Which car are you buying in the first place?

With the average new vehicle transaction price in the U.S. reaching $49,855 in July 2026, choosing a less expensive vehicle can potentially have a much bigger financial impact than shaving a fraction of a percentage point off your loan.

description:
How do you actually think like an investor — instead of a speculator?

Buying stocks doesn’t automatically make you an investor. You can hold a stock for 10 or 20 years and still be speculating if you don’t understand what you own, what it’s worth, what could go wrong, or why you bought it in the first place.

In this video, we break down 5 ways real investors think differently from speculators — and why this distinction may matter more than finding the next hot stock.

We explore some of the most important principles behind intelligent, long-term investing:
